questions.text: Which notation gives an asymptotic upper bound on the running time of an algorithm?
questions.explanation: Big-O bounds the growth of a function from above; Big-Omega bounds it from below and Big-Theta from both sides.

questions.text: What is the Big-O of f(n) = 3n² + 5n + 7?
questions.explanation: The highest-order term 3n² dominates for large n, and constants are dropped, so f(n) = O(n²).

questions.text: Which of these best describes Big-Theta notation?
options: A tight bound: both upper and lower
questions.explanation: f(n) = Θ(g(n)) when g bounds f from above and from below within constant factors.

questions.text: The space complexity of an algorithm is the amount of
options: memory it needs while it runs
questions.explanation: Space complexity measures the memory an algorithm needs as a function of the input size.

questions.text: What is the time complexity of finding the maximum element in an unsorted array of n elements?
questions.explanation: Every element must be looked at once, so the work grows linearly with n.

questions.text: Which growth rate is the slowest for large n?
questions.explanation: log n grows more slowly than √n, n and n log n.

questions.text: Which two operations define the Disjoint Set ADT?
questions.explanation: A disjoint set structure supports Find (which set holds an element) and Union (merge two sets).

questions.text: In a disjoint-set forest, what does 'path compression' do during Find?
options: Makes every node on the path point directly to the root
Sorts the elements of the set
questions.explanation: Path compression re-points the visited nodes to the root, so later Finds on them are faster.

questions.text: Union by rank attaches
options: the taller tree under the shorter one
the shorter tree under the root of the taller one
both trees under a new root
questions.explanation: Attaching the shorter tree below the taller one keeps the trees shallow.

questions.text: With both union by rank and path compression, the amortised cost of each disjoint-set operation is
questions.explanation: Together they give an amortised bound of the inverse Ackermann function α(n), which is below 5 for any practical n.

questions.text: A sparse matrix is a matrix in which
options: the number of rows equals the columns
questions.explanation: When most entries are zero, storing only the non-zero ones saves memory.

questions.text: In the triplet (array) representation of a sparse matrix, each non-zero element is stored as
questions.explanation: Each non-zero entry is kept as its row index, column index and value; the first triplet usually holds the matrix size and count.

questions.text: In row-major order, the address of A[i][j] in an m × n array with base address B and element size w (0-based) is
questions.explanation: In row-major order the i full rows before row i hold i·n elements, then j more elements come before column j.

questions.text: Which language stores two-dimensional arrays in column-major order?
questions.explanation: FORTRAN uses column-major order; C stores arrays row by row.

questions.text: What is the worst-case time of the brute-force string matching algorithm for a text of length n and a pattern of length m?
questions.explanation: For each of the about n starting positions it may compare up to m characters.

questions.text: The Knuth-Morris-Pratt algorithm avoids re-examining text characters by using
options: the failure (prefix) function of the pattern
a suffix tree of the text
questions.explanation: The failure function says how far the pattern can shift after a mismatch, so the text pointer never moves back.

questions.text: The time complexity of KMP string matching is
questions.explanation: Building the prefix table takes O(m) and scanning the text O(n).

questions.text: Which algorithm compares the pattern from right to left and uses bad-character and good-suffix rules?
questions.explanation: Boyer-Moore scans the pattern from its last character and skips ahead using the two heuristics.

questions.text: Rabin-Karp string matching relies on
options: a rolling hash of text windows
questions.explanation: It compares hash values of the pattern and each text window, updating the hash in constant time as the window slides.

questions.text: What is the KMP failure (prefix) function of the pattern 'ABABC'?
questions.explanation: For A,AB,ABA,ABAB,ABABC the longest proper prefix that is also a suffix has length 0,0,1,2,0.

questions.text: What is the worst-case time complexity of Merge Sort?
questions.explanation: Merge Sort always splits in half (log n levels) and merges each level in O(n).

questions.text: What is the worst-case time complexity of Quick Sort with the first element as pivot?
questions.explanation: On an already sorted array each partition removes only the pivot, giving n levels of O(n) work.

questions.text: Which sort is NOT comparison-based?
questions.explanation: Counting Sort counts occurrences of each key value instead of comparing elements.

questions.text: Radix Sort processes the keys
options: digit by digit, using a stable sort for each digit
questions.explanation: LSD Radix Sort sorts on each digit from least to most significant with a stable sort such as Counting Sort.

questions.text: Shell Sort is a generalisation of
questions.explanation: Shell Sort runs insertion sort on elements a gap apart, with the gap shrinking to 1.

questions.text: Tree Sort produces the sorted order by
options: a preorder traversal of a BST
an inorder traversal of a BST
a level-order traversal of a heap
a postorder traversal of an AVL tree
questions.explanation: Inserting all keys into a binary search tree and reading them in inorder gives ascending order.

questions.text: Interpolation search works best when the sorted keys are
questions.explanation: It estimates the position from the key's value, which is accurate when values are spread evenly.

questions.text: Jump Search on a sorted array of n elements uses an optimal block size of
questions.explanation: Jumping √n at a time and then searching linearly within a block gives O(√n) steps.

questions.text: A skip list gives expected search time of
questions.explanation: Its random levels of express lanes halve the remaining distance on average at each level.

questions.text: Which of these sorts is stable?
questions.explanation: Merge Sort keeps equal keys in their original order when it merges from the left half first.

questions.text: Bucket Sort has an average time of O(n + k) when
options: the input is uniformly distributed over the range
the buckets are linked lists of length n
questions.explanation: Uniform input spreads evenly over the buckets, so each holds few elements.

questions.text: An AVL tree is a binary search tree in which the heights of the two subtrees of every node differ by at most
questions.explanation: The balance factor of every node must be -1, 0 or +1.

questions.text: The balance factor of a node in an AVL tree is
options: number of left children − right children
questions.explanation: It is the height of the left subtree minus the height of the right subtree.

questions.text: Inserting into the left subtree of the left child of an unbalanced node needs
questions.explanation: The LL case is fixed by one right rotation about the unbalanced node.

questions.text: The LR imbalance case is fixed by
options: a left rotation on the child, then a right rotation on the node
questions.explanation: LR is a double rotation: rotate the left child left, then the unbalanced node right.

questions.text: What is the worst-case height of an AVL tree with n nodes?
questions.explanation: AVL balancing keeps the height at most about 1.44 log₂ n.

questions.text: Inserting 10, 20, 30 in that order into an empty AVL tree causes which rotation?
questions.explanation: 30 goes to the right of 20, the right of 10; node 10 becomes right-heavy, the RR case, fixed by a left rotation.

questions.text: After deleting a node from an AVL tree, how many rotations may be needed in the worst case?
options: Up to O(log n), one per level
questions.explanation: Unlike insertion, a deletion can unbalance each ancestor in turn, up to the root.

questions.text: In a B-tree of order m, every node has at most
questions.explanation: A node of a B-tree of order m has at most m children and m − 1 keys.

questions.text: Every non-root node of a B-tree of order m has at least
questions.explanation: Nodes other than the root must be at least half full: ⌈m/2⌉ children.

questions.text: In a B+ tree, where are all the data records (or pointers to them) kept?
options: In the leaf nodes, which are linked together
questions.explanation: Internal nodes hold only routing keys; the leaves hold the records and are chained for range scans.

questions.text: A 2-3 tree is a B-tree of order
questions.explanation: Each node of a 2-3 tree has 2 or 3 children, which is a B-tree of order 3.

questions.text: When a key is inserted into a full B-tree node, the node
options: splits, and the middle key moves up to the parent
questions.explanation: A full node splits in two and pushes its median key up, which can split the parent in turn.

questions.text: How does a B* tree differ from a B-tree?
options: It allows nodes to be empty
Nodes are kept at least two-thirds full, sharing keys with a sibling before splitting
Its leaves are not at the same level
questions.explanation: A B* tree redistributes keys to a sibling first and splits two nodes into three, keeping nodes about two-thirds full.

questions.text: Why are B-trees used for database indexes on disk?
options: They use the least memory in RAM
Their high fan-out keeps the tree shallow, so few disk blocks are read
questions.explanation: A node fills a disk block and has many children, so a search reads only a few blocks.
